import type { ComponentProps, MouseEvent, ReactNode } from 'react'
import { Icon } from '@/lib/icon'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './Tag.module.css'

/** Status first, then every hue the accent ramps offer, for categories. */
export const TAG_VARIANTS = [
  'neutral',
  'info',
  'success',
  'warning',
  'danger',
  'red',
  'orange',
  'amber',
  'yellow',
  'lime',
  'green',
  'emerald',
  'teal',
  'cyan',
  'sky',
  'blue',
  'indigo',
  'violet',
  'purple',
  'fuchsia',
  'pink',
  'rose',
] as const
export type TagVariant = (typeof TAG_VARIANTS)[number]

export interface TagProps extends Omit<ComponentProps<'span'>, 'children'> {
  text: string
  startIcon?: ReactNode
  /** Image URL for a small avatar before the text, e.g. a person in a filter. */
  startAvatar?: string
  size?: 'sm' | 'md'
  appearance?: 'subtle' | 'outlined' | 'solid'
  variant?: TagVariant
  hasRemoveButton?: boolean
  onRemove?: (event: MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void
}

export function Tag({
  text,
  startIcon,
  startAvatar,
  size = 'md',
  appearance = 'subtle',
  variant = 'info',
  hasRemoveButton = false,
  onRemove,
  className,
  ...props
}: TagProps) {
  return (
    <span
      className={cn(
        styles.tag,
        styles[size],
        styles[appearance],
        styles[variant],
        className,
      )}
      {...props}
    >
      {startAvatar ? (
        // A plain image, not <Avatar>: the tag only needs a round crop, and a
        // cross-component import would not survive the copy-source install.
        <img src={startAvatar} alt="" className={styles.avatar} />
      ) : (
        startIcon && (
          <span className={styles.icon} aria-hidden="true">
            {startIcon}
          </span>
        )
      )}
      <span className={styles.text}>{text}</span>
      {hasRemoveButton && (
        <button
          type="button"
          // "Remove" alone is ambiguous in a list of tags, each with its own.
          aria-label={`Remove ${text}`}
          className={styles.remove}
          onClick={onRemove}
        >
          <Icon name="close" />
        </button>
      )}
    </span>
  )
}

# Tag A short label that categorises or marks something: a status, a filter chip, a person...
import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TagStories from './Tag.stories'

<Meta of={TagStories} />

# Tag

A short label that categorises or marks something: a status, a filter
chip, a person picked in a field. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/tag](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/tag).

<Canvas of={TagStories.Matrix} />

<Canvas of={TagStories.Colors} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Container** | The box: fill, border and corner by `appearance` and `variant`; the corner follows the Theme's radius. |
| **Start icon** | `startIcon`, sized to the text. Decorative. |
| **Start avatar** | `startAvatar`, a small round image. Decorative (`alt=""`). Replaces the icon when both are given. |
| **Text** | `text`. Truncates with an ellipsis rather than wrapping. |
| **Remove button** | `hasRemoveButton`: a real `<button>` that calls `onRemove`. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | – | Required. |
| `startIcon` | node | – | Usually `<Icon name="…" />`. |
| `startAvatar` | string (URL) | – | |
| `size` | `sm`, `md` | `md` | 20px / 24px tall. |
| `appearance` | `subtle`, `outlined`, `solid` | `subtle` | |
| `variant` | `neutral`, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, or a hue: `red` … `rose` | `info` | Status tokens, or one of the 17 accent hues for categories. See [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs). |
| `hasRemoveButton` | boolean | `false` | |
| `onRemove` | `(event) => void` | – | |

Every other `<span>` attribute passes through to the container.

<Controls of={TagStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **The spec's four variants needed new tokens.** `info`, `success`,
  `warning` and `danger` were added to the token layer for Tag and are
  shared with Alert and Toast.
- **No `isRounded`.** The corner reads `--radius-control`, so it follows
  the Theme's radius preset with every other control, and turns into a
  pill under `radius="full"`.
- **The 17 hue variants are additions.** Each hue has `--<hue>`,
  `-foreground`, `-subtle` and `-text` tokens. Subtle and outlined text is
  measured at 4.5:1 in the token build. Solid is step 600 with a white
  label on every hue, in both appearances, so a row of solid tags reads as
  one set; on the warm hues (orange, amber, yellow, lime and others) that
  label falls below 4.5:1. That is accepted on purpose. Use subtle or
  outlined where the tag has to pass AA.
- **`startAvatar` wins over `startIcon`** if both are passed; the spec
  does not say.
- **The tag does not remove itself.** `onRemove` reports the click and
  the parent drops the tag from its list, so the list stays the one
  source of truth.

## Usage

<Canvas of={TagStories.Sizes} />

<Canvas of={TagStories.RemovableList} />

## Accessibility

- The remove button is named **"Remove `text`"** (e.g. "Remove Design"), so a list of tags does
  not read as a row of identical "Remove" buttons.
- It is a native `<button>`: Tab to reach, Enter or Space to press.
- On touch screens (`pointer: coarse`) its hit area grows to 44×44px
  without changing how the tag looks. That area reaches 10px above and
  below a 24px tag, so in a wrapped list on touch keep at least
  `--space-6` between rows, or neighbouring targets overlap and a tap can
  remove the wrong tag.
- After a tag is removed, focus has nowhere to stay. If that matters, move
  it to the next tag's remove button, or to the field the tags belong to,
  in your `onRemove`.
- Colour carries meaning here, so it must never be the only signal: the
  text says what the status is. The icon and the avatar are decorative.
- Every label and text pair clears 4.5:1 in both themes, and the build
  checks them, except solid hue tags (see above).

import {
  useCallback,
  useLayoutEffect,
  useRef,
  type ComponentProps,
  type CSSProperties,
  type ReactNode,
} from 'react'
import { Field } from '@base-ui/react/field'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import {
  assignRef,
  InputField,
  boxClass,
  focusControl,
  inputStyles,
  type InputSize,
  type ValidationState,
} from './InputField'
import styles from './Textarea.module.css'

export interface TextareaProps extends Omit<ComponentProps<'textarea'>, 'size'> {
  label?: ReactNode
  helperText?: ReactNode
  validationState?: ValidationState
  size?: InputSize
  isFullWidth?: boolean
  /** Which way the user can drag to resize. Ignored with `hasAutoSize`. */
  resize?: 'none' | 'both' | 'vertical' | 'horizontal'
  /** Grow and shrink with the content, between `minRows` and `maxRows`. */
  hasAutoSize?: boolean
  /** The starting height, in lines. */
  minRows?: number
  /** The most it grows to before scrolling, in lines. */
  maxRows?: number
}

export function Textarea({
  label,
  helperText,
  validationState,
  size = 'md',
  isFullWidth,
  resize = 'vertical',
  hasAutoSize = false,
  minRows = 3,
  maxRows,
  required,
  disabled,
  name,
  className,
  onInput,
  ref,
  style,
  ...props
}: TextareaProps) {
  const inner = useRef<HTMLTextAreaElement | null>(null)
  const fit = useCallback(() => {
    const el = inner.current
    if (!el || !hasAutoSize) return
    // Collapse first so a shrinking value can shrink the box; max-block-size
    // (from maxRows) caps the result and the rest scrolls.
    el.style.blockSize = 'auto'
    el.style.blockSize = `${el.scrollHeight}px`
  }, [hasAutoSize])
  // Controlled values change without an input event; fit to those too.
  useLayoutEffect(fit, [fit, props.value])

  return (
    <InputField
      label={label}
      helperText={helperText}
      validationState={validationState}
      required={required}
      disabled={disabled}
      name={name}
      isFullWidth={isFullWidth}
      className={className}
    >
      <span className={cn(boxClass(size), styles.multiline, styles[`pad-${size}`])} onMouseDown={focusControl}>
        <Field.Control
          render={
            <textarea
              rows={minRows}
              ref={(node) => {
                inner.current = node
                assignRef(ref, node)
              }}
            />
          }
          {...(props as ComponentProps<typeof Field.Control>)}
          required={required}
          onInput={(event) => {
            fit()
            onInput?.(event as unknown as Parameters<NonNullable<TextareaProps["onInput"]>>[0])
          }}
          className={cn(inputStyles.control, styles.textarea)}
          style={
            {
              ...style,
              resize: hasAutoSize ? 'none' : resize,
              ...(maxRows && { maxBlockSize: `calc(${maxRows} * 1lh + 2 * var(--pad-block))` }),
            } as CSSProperties
          }
        />
      </span>
    </InputField>
  )
}

# Textarea Several lines of text: a message, a description, a note. Spec: [uiguideline.com...
import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TextareaStories from './Textarea.stories'

<Meta of={TextareaStories} />

# Textarea

Several lines of text: a message, a description, a note. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/textarea](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/textarea).
The same field as [Text Input](?path=/docs/components-inputs-textinput--docs):
label, helper, validation and sizes are shared. Outlined only.

<Canvas of={TextareaStories.Sizes} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Label** | `label`, above the field. |
| **Field** | The box: edge, fill and focus ring, padded top and bottom so it grows with the text. |
| **Placeholder** | `placeholder`. |
| **Resize handle** | The browser's own, in the field's bottom corner, on the axes `resize` allows. Hidden with `hasAutoSize`. |
| **Helper text** | `helperText`; the error message when `validationState` is error. |

## Props

Everything Text Input takes except `prefix`, `suffix` and `appearance`, plus:

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `resize` | `none`, `both`, `vertical`, `horizontal` | `vertical` | |
| `hasAutoSize` | boolean | `false` | Grows and shrinks with the text. |
| `minRows` | number | `3` | Starting height (the `rows` attribute). |
| `maxRows` | number | – | Where auto-size stops and scrolling starts. |

`onChange` is the native event; every other `<textarea>` attribute passes
through, including `ref`.

<Controls of={TextareaStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- Native `disabled`, `required`, `readOnly` names, and native `onChange`,
  as on Text Input.
- **`minRows` defaults to 3.** The spec gives none; the browser's own
  default of 2 is too short to read as a multi-line field.

## Usage

<Canvas of={TextareaStories.AutoSize} />

Use auto-size for text whose length varies a lot, with a `maxRows` so the
page does not grow without limit. Keep the manual handle (`vertical`) when
people may want to see more at once.

## Accessibility

- A real `<textarea>` with its `<label>`, the helper as its description,
  and `aria-invalid` in the error state.
- Edge is the light `--field-border` (about 1.5:1, see Text Input); focus ring around the
  whole field.
- Enter inserts a line break; it does not submit the form.
- Auto-size caps at `maxRows` and scrolls beyond it, so a long entry never
  pushes the rest of the form off screen.

import type { ComponentProps, ReactNode } from 'react'
import { Field } from '@base-ui/react/field'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import {
  InputField,
  boxClass,
  focusControl,
  inputStyles,
  type InputSize,
  type ValidationState,
} from './InputField'

export interface TextInputProps extends Omit<ComponentProps<'input'>, 'size' | 'prefix'> {
  label?: ReactNode
  /** Under the field; the error message when `validationState` is error. */
  helperText?: ReactNode
  validationState?: ValidationState
  size?: InputSize
  /** Text or an icon before the value, e.g. `<Icon name="search" />` or "https://". */
  prefix?: ReactNode
  /** Text or an icon after the value, e.g. "kg". */
  suffix?: ReactNode
  isFullWidth?: boolean
}

export function TextInput({
  label,
  helperText,
  validationState,
  size = 'md',
  prefix,
  suffix,
  isFullWidth,
  required,
  disabled,
  name,
  className,
  ...props
}: TextInputProps) {
  return (
    <InputField
      label={label}
      helperText={helperText}
      validationState={validationState}
      required={required}
      disabled={disabled}
      name={name}
      isFullWidth={isFullWidth}
      className={className}
    >
      <span className={boxClass(size)} onMouseDown={focusControl}>
        {prefix && <span className={inputStyles.affix}>{prefix}</span>}
        <Field.Control {...props} required={required} className={cn(inputStyles.control)} />
        {suffix && <span className={inputStyles.affix}>{suffix}</span>}
      </span>
    </InputField>
  )
}

# Text Input A single line of text: a name, an email, a URL. Spec: [uiguideline.com/compon...
import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TextInputStories from './TextInput.stories'

<Meta of={TextInputStories} />

# Text Input

A single line of text: a name, an email, a URL. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/text-input](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/text-input).
Label, description and invalid state are wired by Base UI's
[Field](https://base-ui.com/react/components/field).

<Canvas of={TextInputStories.Default} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Label** | `label`, above the field. Clicking it focuses the input. |
| **Field** | The box that draws the edge, fill and focus ring. |
| **Prefix** / **Suffix** | `prefix`, `suffix`: text or an icon inside the field, in the muted colour. |
| **Placeholder** | `placeholder`. A hint, never a replacement for the label. |
| **Helper text** | `helperText`, under the field. The error message when `validationState` is error. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | node | – | |
| `helperText` | node | – | |
| `validationState` | `default`, `success`, `error` | `default` | |
| `size` | `sm`, `md` | `md` | 24, 32px. |
| `prefix`, `suffix` | node | – | |
| `isFullWidth` | boolean | `false` | Otherwise 20rem, capped at its container. |
| `value`, `defaultValue`, `onChange` | | – | As on `<input>`: `onChange` gets the event. |
| `placeholder`, `name`, `pattern`, `maxLength`, `type`, `autoFocus` | | – | Native. |
| `disabled`, `required`, `readOnly` | boolean | `false` | Native. |

Every other `<input>` attribute passes through to the input, including `ref`.

<Controls of={TextInputStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **No `filled` appearance.** The spec's filled field (a tinted box with a bottom rule) was dropped to match the Claude apps, where every field is the white outlined box.
- **Two sizes, not three.** `sm` (24px) and `md` (32px) only, the compact control scale of the Claude apps. The spec's larger steps were dropped; a big call to action is `md` with more room around it, not a taller box.
- **Native names** for native attributes: `disabled`, `required`,
  `readOnly` rather than `isDisabled`, `isRequired`, `isReadOnly`.
- **`onChange` is the native event**, not a value: the kit's rule for
  components that wrap a real input, so it works with every form library
  as-is.
- **Changed in 0.8:** `error` became `validationState="error"` plus
  `helperText`; `forwardRef` is gone (`ref` is a prop in React 19).

## Usage

<Canvas of={TextInputStories.Sizes} />

<Canvas of={TextInputStories.PrefixSuffix} />

<Canvas of={TextInputStories.Validation} />

## Accessibility

- The label is a real `<label>` for the input; the helper is its
  description (`aria-describedby`); the error state sets `aria-invalid`.
  Do not rely on the placeholder as a label: it disappears as soon as
  anyone types.
- **The edge is `--field-border`, about 1.5:1 — a deliberate exception
  to WCAG 1.4.11** (approved 2026-10-08), for the light hairline of the
  Claude apps. The outlined field is a white `--card` box with a faint
  drop on the off-white page, and the label, placeholder and focus ring
  mark it too. Low-vision users may still find the box hard to see; if
  your audience needs 3:1, set `--field-border: var(--control-border)`.
- Focus draws a 2px ring around the whole field (in the danger colour
  when invalid), on click as well as keyboard, since that is where typing
  goes.
- Pressing the field's padding or a prefix focuses the input, like a
  native field.
- Heights are 24 or 32px, 44px hit area on touch; the label is part of the target too.

import { useSyncExternalStore, type ReactNode } from 'react'
import { Toast as BaseToast } from '@base-ui/react/toast'
import { Icon, type IconName } from '@/lib/icon'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './Toast.module.css'

export type ToastVariant = 'default' | 'info' | 'success' | 'warning' | 'danger'

export interface ToastOptions {
  title?: ReactNode
  description?: ReactNode
  variant?: ToastVariant
  /** One button, e.g. "Undo". Keep the same action reachable elsewhere: the toast goes away. */
  action?: { label: ReactNode; onClick: () => void }
  /** Milliseconds before it closes; `0` keeps it until dismissed. */
  timeout?: number
  /** `high` interrupts the screen reader (danger defaults to it). */
  priority?: 'low' | 'high'
  onClose?: () => void
}

export interface ToastProviderProps {
  children: ReactNode
  placement?: 'top-left' | 'top-center' | 'top-right' | 'bottom-left' | 'bottom-center' | 'bottom-right'
  /** Default time on screen, in milliseconds. */
  timeout?: number
  /** Toasts shown at once; older ones wait. */
  limit?: number
}

// Base UI's promise() sets these types itself.
const variantOf = (type: string | undefined): ToastVariant | 'loading' =>
  type === 'error' ? 'danger' : type === 'loading' ? 'loading' : ((type as ToastVariant) ?? 'default')

const icons: Partial<Record<ToastVariant, IconName>> = {
  info: 'info-filled',
  success: 'success-filled',
  warning: 'warning-filled',
  danger: 'danger-filled',
}

// The toast takes the opposite appearance of the page (dark on a light page,
// light on a dark one) so it stands out from what is under it. The page's
// appearance is the `dark` class on <html>.
const subscribeToPageTheme = (onChange: () => void) => {
  const observer = new MutationObserver(onChange)
  observer.observe(document.documentElement, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['class'] })
  return () => observer.disconnect()
}
const pageIsDark = () => document.documentElement.classList.contains('dark')

function ToastList({ swipe }: { swipe: 'left' | 'right' | 'up' | 'down' }) {
  const { toasts } = BaseToast.useToastManager()
  return toasts.map((toast) => {
    const variant = variantOf(toast.type)
    const icon = variant === 'loading' ? null : icons[variant]
    return (
      <BaseToast.Root
        key={toast.id}
        toast={toast}
        swipeDirection={swipe}
        // Each toast is a (non-modal) dialog and needs a name. promise()
        // passes its strings as the description, with no title: name it by
        // what it says rather than leave it unnamed.
        aria-label={toast.title ? undefined : typeof toast.description === 'string' ? toast.description : 'Notification'}
        className={cn(styles.toast, styles[variant])}
      >
        {variant === 'loading' && <span className={cn(styles.icon, styles.spinner)} aria-hidden="true" />}
        {icon && (
          <span className={styles.icon} aria-hidden="true">
            <Icon name={icon} />
          </span>
        )}
        <BaseToast.Content className={styles.content}>
          {toast.title && <BaseToast.Title className={styles.title} />}
          {toast.description && <BaseToast.Description className={styles.description} />}
          {toast.actionProps && <BaseToast.Action className={styles.action} />}
        </BaseToast.Content>
        <BaseToast.Close aria-label="Dismiss" className={styles.close}>
          <Icon name="close" />
        </BaseToast.Close>
      </BaseToast.Root>
    )
  })
}

/** Wrap the app once. Toasts render in a corner of the viewport, above everything. */
export function ToastProvider({ children, placement = 'bottom-right', timeout = 5000, limit = 3 }: ToastProviderProps) {
  const [vertical, horizontal] = placement.split('-') as ['top' | 'bottom', 'left' | 'center' | 'right']
  const swipe = horizontal === 'center' ? (vertical === 'top' ? 'up' : 'down') : horizontal
  const dark = useSyncExternalStore(subscribeToPageTheme, pageIsDark, () => false)
  return (
    <BaseToast.Provider timeout={timeout} limit={limit}>
      {children}
      <BaseToast.Portal>
        <BaseToast.Viewport className={cn(styles.viewport, styles[vertical], styles[horizontal], dark ? 'light' : 'dark')}>
          <ToastList swipe={swipe} />
        </BaseToast.Viewport>
      </BaseToast.Portal>
    </BaseToast.Provider>
  )
}

/** Show, update and close toasts from anywhere inside a ToastProvider. */
export function useToast() {
  const manager = BaseToast.useToastManager()
  // Only the fields that were given: Base UI merges an update over the
  // toast, so an explicit undefined would wipe its variant or action.
  const toOptions = ({ variant, action, priority, ...rest }: ToastOptions) => {
    const options: Record<string, unknown> = { ...rest }
    if (variant !== undefined) options.type = variant
    const p = priority ?? (variant === 'danger' ? 'high' : undefined)
    if (p !== undefined) options.priority = p
    if (action !== undefined) options.actionProps = { children: action.label, onClick: action.onClick }
    return options
  }
  return {
    /** Returns the toast's id. */
    add: (options: ToastOptions) => manager.add(toOptions(options)),
    update: (id: string, options: ToastOptions) => manager.update(id, toOptions(options)),
    /** Closes one toast, or every toast without an id. */
    close: (id?: string) => manager.close(id),
    /** A loading toast that turns into success or danger when the promise settles. */
    promise: manager.promise,
  }
}

# Toast A short message in a corner of the screen about something that just happened: save...
import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ToastStories from './Toast.stories'

<Meta of={ToastStories} />

# Toast

A short message in a corner of the screen about something that just
happened: saved, sent, moved, failed. It closes itself after a few
seconds and never blocks the page. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/toast](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/toast).
Behaviour from Base UI's [Toast](https://base-ui.com/react/components/toast).

<Canvas of={ToastStories.Default} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Icon** | The variant's filled icon in its text colour; none for `default`, a spinner while a promise is pending. |
| **Title** | Semibold. What happened. |
| **Description** | Optional, `--muted-foreground`. |
| **Action** | Optional, one text button, e.g. "Undo". |
| **Close button** | Always there. |

The surface is `--popover` with `--shadow-lg`, at most 24rem wide, in the
opposite appearance to the page: dark toasts on a light page, light on a
dark one.

## API

Wrap the app once in `ToastProvider`, then call `useToast()` anywhere
inside it:

```tsx
<ToastProvider placement="bottom-right">
  <App />
</ToastProvider>

const toast = useToast()
toast.add({ title: 'File moved to Trash', action: { label: 'Undo', onClick: restore } })
```

| `ToastProvider` prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `placement` | `top-` or `bottom-` + `left`, `center`, `right` | `bottom-right` | |
| `timeout` | number (ms) | `5000` | Default time on screen. |
| `limit` | number | `3` | Shown at once; the rest wait. |

| `useToast()` | |
| --- | --- |
| `add(options)` | Shows a toast, returns its id. |
| `update(id, options)` | Changes one in place. |
| `close(id?)` | Closes one, or all. |
| `promise(promise, { loading, success, error })` | A loading toast that becomes success or danger when the promise settles. |

| Option | Values | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title`, `description` | node | |
| `variant` | `default`, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger` | |
| `action` | `{ label, onClick }` | |
| `timeout` | number (ms) | `0` keeps it until dismissed. |
| `priority` | `low`, `high` | `high` by default for `danger`. |
| `onClose` | function | |

<Controls of={ToastStories.Default} />

### Design notes

- **Inverted appearance.** The viewport carries `.dark` when `<html>` is
  light and `.light` when it is `.dark`, and follows the page if it
  switches while a toast is open. The contrast with the page pulls the eye
  to a message that is only there for a few seconds. A `Theme` with its own
  `appearance` deeper in the tree does not reach the toast: it renders in a
  portal on `<body>`.
- **The variant colours only the icon.** The message stays in
  `--popover-foreground`, the same as Alert's subtle and outlined
  appearances: a toast is read in passing, and body text in an accent
  colour reads worse.
- **Above everything, at z-index 70**, over popups (50) and tooltips
  (60): a toast raised from inside a modal shows over the modal and is
  not hidden from assistive tech by it.

  <Canvas of={ToastStories.FromModal} />

- **Swipe to dismiss** toward the nearest edge on touch.

## Usage

<Canvas of={ToastStories.Variants} />

<Canvas of={ToastStories.PromiseToast} />

<Canvas of={ToastStories.Timeout} />

<Canvas of={ToastStories.TopCenter} />

A toast disappears. Anything the reader must act on, or might need to
read twice, belongs in an Alert on the page or a Modal; the action on a
toast ("Undo") should also be reachable some other way.

## Accessibility

- The viewport is a polite live region: new toasts are announced
  without interrupting. `danger` toasts (and any with `priority: 'high'`)
  are `role="alertdialog"` and announced assertively.
- Each toast is a non-modal dialog named by its title, or by its
  description when it has none (as `promise()` toasts do).
- Timers pause while the pointer is over the toasts or focus is in
  them, so there is time to reach the action. F6 moves focus to the
  toast region.
- The close button is named `Dismiss` and has a 44px touch target on
  coarse pointers.

import type { ComponentProps, ReactNode, Ref } from 'react'
import { Toggle } from '@base-ui/react/toggle'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import { Button, type ButtonProps } from './Button'
import styles from './ToggleButton.module.css'

interface ToggleButtonBaseProps
  extends Omit<ComponentProps<'button'>, 'ref' | 'value' | 'defaultValue' | 'onChange'> {
  // Always a <button> (Button itself may be an <a>, hence its wider type).
  ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>
  /** Colour of the pressed state. Unpressed is always neutral. */
  variant?: ButtonProps['variant']
  /** Style of the pressed state. */
  appearance?: ButtonProps['appearance']
  size?: ButtonProps['size']
  startIcon?: ReactNode
  endIcon?: ReactNode
  isLoading?: boolean
  isFullWidth?: boolean
  /** Controlled pressed state (the spec's `isSelected`). */
  pressed?: boolean
  defaultPressed?: boolean
  /** Base UI's second argument (event details) is dropped: nothing here needs it. */
  onPressedChange?: (pressed: boolean) => void
  /** Identifies the toggle inside a group. */
  value?: string
}

/** An icon-only toggle has no text to name it, so `aria-label` is required. */
export type ToggleButtonProps =
  | (ToggleButtonBaseProps & { isIconOnly?: false })
  | (ToggleButtonBaseProps & { isIconOnly: true; 'aria-label': string })

export function ToggleButton({
  variant = 'primary',
  appearance = 'contained',
  size,
  startIcon,
  endIcon,
  isLoading,
  isFullWidth,
  isIconOnly,
  pressed,
  defaultPressed,
  onPressedChange,
  disabled,
  className,
  children,
  ...props
}: ToggleButtonProps) {
  return (
    <Toggle
      {...props}
      pressed={pressed}
      defaultPressed={defaultPressed}
      onPressedChange={onPressedChange && ((next) => onPressedChange(next))}
      disabled={disabled}
      render={(toggleProps, state) => {
        const buttonProps = {
          ...toggleProps,
          // Off is the same neutral button whatever the pressed style is, so
          // "on" is always the one that stands out.
          variant: state.pressed ? variant : 'secondary',
          appearance: state.pressed ? appearance : appearance === 'ghost' ? 'ghost' : 'outlined',
          size,
          startIcon,
          endIcon,
          isLoading,
          isFullWidth,
          // Its aria-label reached Toggle with the other props and comes back
          // in toggleProps, which is what Button's icon-only type asks for.
          isIconOnly,
          disabled,
          className: cn(state.pressed && appearance !== 'contained' && styles.tinted, className),
          children,
        } as ButtonProps
        return <Button {...buttonProps} />
      }}
    />
  )
}

# Toggle Button A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter ap...
import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ToggleButtonStories from './ToggleButton.stories'

<Meta of={ToggleButtonStories} />

# Toggle Button

A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter
applied or not. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/toggle-button](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/toggle-button).
Behaviour from Base UI's [Toggle](https://base-ui.com/react/components/toggle);
the look is [Button](?path=/docs/components-buttons-button--docs)'s.

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Matrix} />

## Anatomy

The same parts as Button — **container**, **start icon**, **label**, **end
icon**, **spinner** — plus one state: **pressed**.

| State | Looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Unpressed | Always neutral: `secondary outlined` (or `ghost` when the appearance is ghost). |
| Pressed, `contained` | The variant's solid fill. |
| Pressed, `outlined` | The variant's border on the neutral secondary fill. |
| Pressed, `ghost` | The neutral secondary fill. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pressed` | boolean | – | Controlled. The spec's `isSelected`. |
| `defaultPressed` | boolean | `false` | Uncontrolled starting state. |
| `onPressedChange` | `(pressed) => void` | – | |
| `variant` | `primary`, `accent`, `secondary`, `destructive` | `primary` | Colour of the pressed state. |
| `appearance` | `contained`, `outlined`, `ghost` | `contained` | Style of the pressed state. |
| `size` | `sm`, `md` | `md` | 24, 32px, as on Button. |
| `startIcon`, `endIcon` | node | – | |
| `isIconOnly` | boolean | `false` | Requires `aria-label`. |
| `isLoading` | boolean | `false` | |
| `isFullWidth` | boolean | `false` | |
| `disabled` | boolean | `false` | |
| `onClick` | function | – | |

<Controls of={ToggleButtonStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **Two sizes, not four.** `sm` (24px) and `md` (32px) only, the compact control scale of the Claude apps. The spec's larger steps were dropped; a big call to action is `md` with more room around it, not a taller box.
- **`pressed`, `defaultPressed`, `onPressedChange`** instead of
  `isSelected`: Base UI's names, per the kit's convention for components
  built on it. "Pressed" is also the ARIA word (`aria-pressed`).
- **`disabled`**, not `isDisabled`.
- **`variant` and `appearance` describe the pressed state.** The spec
  applies them to the button without saying what changes when it is
  selected. If unpressed also took them, a contained toggle would look
  pressed whether it was or not.
- **A pressed outlined or ghost toggle is filled neutral, not tinted with
  its variant.** It stays in that state indefinitely, so its label has to
  pass 4.5:1 on the fill — and red text on a red tint measures 3.7:1.
- **`isIconOnly`**, as on Button.

## Usage

Use a toggle for a setting that is on or off and applies immediately.
If the choice is submitted with a form, use a Checkbox or Switch instead.
For one-of-many, use a group of radios or tabs.

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.IconOnly} />

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Controlled} />

## Accessibility

- A native `<button>` with `aria-pressed`, so a screen reader announces
  "Subscribe, toggle button, pressed".
- **Keep the label the same in both states.** `aria-pressed` carries the
  state; a label that switches from "Follow" to "Unfollow" as well reads
  as "Unfollow, pressed", which contradicts itself.
- Enter and Space both toggle it.
- `isLoading` keeps it focusable but inert, as on Button.
- 44×44px touch target at `sm` and `md`, from Button.

import { useId, useState, type ReactElement, type ReactNode } from 'react'
import { Tooltip as BaseTooltip } from '@base-ui/react/tooltip'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './Tooltip.module.css'

export interface TooltipProps {
  /** What the tooltip says. Short: a label or a hint, never the only way to learn something essential. */
  content: ReactNode
  /** The trigger: one focusable element, such as a Button. Its props are merged, not wrapped. */
  children: ReactElement
  side?: 'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left'
  align?: 'start' | 'center' | 'end'
  /** Milliseconds of hover before it opens. Focus opens it at once. */
  delay?: number
  closeDelay?: number
  open?: boolean
  defaultOpen?: boolean
  onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void
  /** Never open, e.g. while the trigger's label is already visible. */
  disabled?: boolean
  className?: string
}

export function Tooltip({
  content,
  children,
  side = 'top',
  align = 'center',
  delay = 300,
  closeDelay = 0,
  open: openProp,
  defaultOpen = false,
  onOpenChange,
  disabled = false,
  className,
}: TooltipProps) {
  const id = useId()
  const [openState, setOpenState] = useState(defaultOpen)
  const open = openProp ?? openState
  return (
    <BaseTooltip.Root
      open={open}
      onOpenChange={(next) => {
        setOpenState(next)
        onOpenChange?.(next)
      }}
      disabled={disabled}
    >
      <BaseTooltip.Trigger
        delay={delay}
        closeDelay={closeDelay}
        render={children}
        // Base UI leaves tooltips out of the accessibility tree; while one is
        // open, point the trigger at it so it is read as a description.
        aria-describedby={open ? id : undefined}
      />
      <BaseTooltip.Portal>
        <BaseTooltip.Positioner className={styles.positioner} side={side} align={align} sideOffset={6}>
          <BaseTooltip.Popup id={id} role="tooltip" className={cn(styles.popup, className)}>
            {content}
          </BaseTooltip.Popup>
        </BaseTooltip.Positioner>
      </BaseTooltip.Portal>
    </BaseTooltip.Root>
  )
}

/** Tooltips inside share one delay: once one has opened, moving to the next opens it at once. */
export const TooltipGroup = BaseTooltip.Provider

# Tooltip A short label that appears when you hover over or focus a control: the name of a...
import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TooltipStories from './Tooltip.stories'

<Meta of={TooltipStories} />

# Tooltip

A short label that appears when you hover over or focus a control: the
name of an icon-only button, a keyboard shortcut, a one-line hint. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/tooltip](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/tooltip).
Behaviour from Base UI's [Tooltip](https://base-ui.com/react/components/tooltip).

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.LongContent} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Trigger** | `children`: one focusable element. Tooltip merges its props onto it rather than wrapping it. |
| **Popup** | Inverted: `--foreground` behind `--background` text, `body-sm`, at most 20rem wide. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `content` | node | – | Required. |
| `children` | element | – | Required. The trigger. |
| `side` | `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left` | `top` | Flips if there is no room. |
| `align` | `start`, `center`, `end` | `center` | |
| `delay` | number (ms) | `300` | Hover delay. Focus opens it at once. |
| `closeDelay` | number (ms) | `0` | |
| `open`, `defaultOpen`, `onOpenChange` | | | Controlled or uncontrolled. |
| `disabled` | boolean | `false` | Never opens. |

`TooltipGroup` (Base UI's `Tooltip.Provider`) wraps several tooltips so
that once one has opened, moving to the next opens it without the delay:

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.Group} />

<Controls of={TooltipStories.Default} />

### Design notes

- **Inverted in both modes.** A tooltip is not part of the page; the
  dark-on-light (light-on-dark in dark mode) box says so, at the same
  contrast as body text.
- **300ms before it opens on hover.** Quick enough to feel responsive,
  long enough that tooltips do not flash as the pointer crosses a toolbar; `TooltipGroup` removes the wait once the
  reader is clearly browsing tooltips.

## Usage

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.Default} />

Only one tooltip is open at a time: opening one closes any other. Hover
or focus the trigger above to see them.

Keep it to a label or a hint. Anything a reader needs in order to finish
a task belongs on the page: a tooltip cannot be reached by touch, and it
disappears the moment you look away. For interactive content, use a
Popover.

## Accessibility

- It opens on hover after `delay` and on keyboard focus at once, and
  closes on Escape, blur or pointer leave.
- Base UI keeps tooltips out of the accessibility tree. This component
  gives the popup `role="tooltip"` and, while it is open, points the
  trigger's `aria-describedby` at it, so it is read as a description.
- It is a **description, not a name.** An icon-only button still needs
  its own `aria-label`; the tooltip then shows that label to sighted
  users too.
- The trigger must be focusable. A disabled button is not, so its
  tooltip never opens by keyboard: put the reason it is disabled in text
  next to it instead.
- Hover and touch cannot reach the tooltip content, so it must never hold
  a link or a button.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import docs from './docs.module.css'

const BREAKPOINTS = [
  { name: 'base', min: '0', px: '0px' },
  { name: 'sm', min: '40rem', px: '640px' },
  { name: 'md', min: '48rem', px: '768px' },
  { name: 'lg', min: '64rem', px: '1024px' },
  { name: 'xl', min: '80rem', px: '1280px' },
  { name: '2xl', min: '96rem', px: '1536px' },
] as const

// One row per breakpoint; each hides itself once the next one is reached, so
// exactly one is visible and it is the active one. Resize the preview to see
// it change.
const ACTIVE = [
  docs.bpBase,
  docs.bpSm,
  docs.bpMd,
  docs.bpLg,
  docs.bpXl,
  docs.bp2xl,
] as const

function ActiveBreakpoint() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {BREAKPOINTS.map((bp, i) => (
        <div key={bp.name} className={`${ACTIVE[i]} ${docs.bpChip}`}>
          <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body)', fontWeight: 500 }}>
            {bp.name}
          </span>
          <span style={{ fontSize: 'var(--text-body-sm)', opacity: 0.8 }}>
            active from {bp.min} ({bp.px}) up
          </span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function Ladder() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {BREAKPOINTS.filter((b) => b.name !== 'base').map((bp) => (
        <div key={bp.name} className={docs.row} style={{ gap: 'var(--space-3)' }}>
          <span className={docs.caption} style={{ width: '2.5rem', flexShrink: 0 }}>{bp.name}</span>
          <div
            style={{
              height: '1rem',
              borderRadius: 'var(--radius-sm)',
              background: 'var(--muted)',
              width: `calc(${bp.min} / 96 * 100%)`,
            }}
          />
          <span className={docs.caption}>{bp.px}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Breakpoints Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without modifi...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as BreakpointsStories from './Breakpoints.stories'

<Meta of={BreakpointsStories} />

# Breakpoints

Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without
modification. Zweihänder declares no `--breakpoint-*` of its own.

| Prefix | Min width | At a 16px root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | `0` | 0px |
| `sm:` | `40rem` | 640px |
| `md:` | `48rem` | 768px |
| `lg:` | `64rem` | 1024px |
| `xl:` | `80rem` | 1280px |
| `2xl:` | `96rem` | 1536px |

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Scale} />

The box below reports the breakpoint currently in effect. Resize the
preview — or use Storybook's viewport toolbar — and it changes.

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Active} />

## They are min-width, and that has a direction

`md:flex` means "flex at 768px **and above**". There is no maximum, so
rules outside a media query are the small-screen case and every
`@media (width >= …)` is an override for larger screens. Write the phone
layout first and widen it; writing the desktop layout first means every
breakpoint has to undo something.

The other direction is expressible — `@media (width < 48rem)` caps a rule
below a breakpoint — but mixing both in one component is where responsive
CSS usually becomes unreadable. Pick min-width and stay there.

## Breakpoints are in rem

`40rem`, not `640px`. A reader who raises their browser's default font
size gets the layout to break earlier, because the layout responds to how
large the text actually is rather than to the device. That is the correct
behaviour and it is worth not overriding: a `px` breakpoint holds a
multi-column layout together long after its text has stopped fitting.

The px column above is only true at the default 16px root.

## The kit has no opinion yet

**No component here uses a breakpoint.** Controls such as Button and Text
Input are inline-sized — they fill whatever their container gives them and have no
layout of their own to rearrange. The stories on this page are the only
responsive code in the repo.

That is expected at this stage: breakpoints are a **layout** concern, and
layout is the [Patterns](?path=/docs/patterns-overview--docs) tier, which
is empty. Marketing sections, dashboards and checkout flows are where
these will actually get used, and where the kit will need an opinion about
which of the five are load-bearing. Most design systems end up leaning on
two or three.

## Container queries are usually the better tool

A breakpoint asks how wide the *viewport* is. A component almost always
wants to know how wide **its own container** is — the same card is narrow
in a sidebar and wide in a main column at one identical viewport width.

Container queries are in every current browser, and they are plain CSS:

```css
.card {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.cardBody {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

@container (width >= 28rem) {
  .cardBody {
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}
```

When a component is built here that needs to reflow, it should reach for
`@container` first and a viewport breakpoint only when the thing being
arranged really is the page.

## Customization

Breakpoints are theme keys like any other, redefined in the `@theme`
block:

```css
@theme {
  --breakpoint-sm: 30rem;
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;
}
```

Two cautions. These generate utility *variants*, so they cannot be
overridden per-scope by `Theme` the way a color can — a variant is
compiled into a media query at build time, and there is no runtime
variable to swap. And removing a default breakpoint removes its prefix
entirely, so any existing `lg:` becomes a silent no-op rather than an
error.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import docs from './docs.module.css'
import { PALETTE, STEPS } from './palette'

function BandSwatches({ pairs }: { pairs: readonly (readonly [string, string])[] }) {
  return (
    <div className={docs.grid}>
      {pairs.map(([bg, fg]) => (
        <div
          key={bg}
          className={docs.swatchPair}
          style={{ background: `var(--${bg})`, color: `var(--${fg})` }}
        >
          <span className={docs.swatchLabel}>--{bg}</span>
          <span className={docs.swatchLabel}>--{fg}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

const LINES = ['border', 'input', 'ring'] as const

function LineSwatches() {
  return (
    <div style={{ display: 'flex', gap: 'var(--space-6)' }}>
      {LINES.map((token) => (
        <div
          key={token}
          style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', alignItems: 'center', gap: 'var(--space-2)' }}
        >
          <div
            style={{
              height: '2.5rem',
              width: '6rem',
              borderRadius: 'var(--radius-md)',
              boxShadow: `inset 0 0 0 2px var(--${token})`,
            }}
          />
          <span className={docs.caption}>--{token}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function PrimitiveSwatches() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {Object.entries(PALETTE).map(([hue, values]) => (
        <div key={hue} className={docs.rampRow}>
          <span className={docs.rampName}>{hue}</span>
          <div className={docs.ramp}>
            {values.map((value, i) => (
              <div
                key={STEPS[i]}
                title={`${hue}-${STEPS[i]}`}
                className={docs.rampStep}
                style={{ background: value }}
              />
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Colors Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in `src/tokens.css`, ...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ColorsStories from './Colors.stories'

<Meta of={ColorsStories} />

# Colors

Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in
`src/tokens.css`, with a counterpart under the `.dark` class. There is no
separate dark palette file and no JS theme object — one stylesheet holds
both modes.

**Read them with `var()`** — `background: var(--card)`,
`color: var(--muted-foreground)`, `border-color: var(--border)`. Because
the variable changes rather than the rule, a component written this way
switches theme without a single conditional: there is no light branch and
no dark branch anywhere in the kit's CSS.

**The swatches below read their values out of the live document**, so a
color shown here is the value the components actually get. The token
*names* are still listed by hand in `Colors.stories.tsx`, though — add a
token to `tokens.css` and it will not appear here until it is added there
too.

## Surfaces

`--background` is the page. `--card` and `--popover` are surfaces that sit
a level above it — a card inset in the page, a menu floating over it. In
light mode the page is gray-50, a cool off-white, and card/popover are
white: a panel separates from the page by being lighter, so it needs a
border at most, not a shadow. In dark mode `--background` sits at the
darkest step and card/popover are lifted one step toward the viewer.

Each surface has a `-foreground` partner, and the pair is the contract:
put `--card-foreground` on `--card`, never `--foreground`, even where the
two happen to be equal today.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Surfaces} />

## Subtle surfaces

`--muted` and `--accent` are the same value in both modes and differ only
in intent. `--muted` is for surfaces that recede — a disabled field's
fill, a table's zebra stripe — and is the only one of the two with a
foreground meant for *long-form* secondary text. `--accent` is for
surfaces that are reacting to the user: hover on a menu item, the
selected row in a list.

They are interchangeable in appearance, so nothing breaks visually if you
swap them, and nothing tells you that you did. The distinction is the
whole point: when a brand color eventually replaces one of them, only the
intent that should change will change.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SubtleSurfaces} />

## Solid actions

Filled controls. `--primary` is the default button and **the brand hue** —
blue out of the box, and the one token the
[`accentColor`](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) setting moves. It
lightens in dark mode rather than darkening, so `--primary-foreground`
inverts with it.

`--destructive` is a hue too, but a fixed one: it stays red whatever the
accent is. A status colour that follows the brand stops being a status —
if the accent is already red, distinguish destructive actions by wording
and placement, not by colour alone.

A note on names: the token called `--accent` is **not** the brand hue. It
is a subtle surface (hover, selected row). The brand hue is `--primary`.
The collision is unfortunate and predates this kit — the names come from
the token contract the registry is compatible with.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SolidActions} />

## Lines and focus

`--border` is a divider or a container edge, `--input` is a form control's
edge, `--ring` is the focus indicator. None of them take a foreground —
they are only ever an outline color, never a fill behind text.

`--border` and `--input` are the same value in both modes and, like
muted/accent, are separated by intent rather than appearance. In dark mode
they stop being opaque neutrals and become white at 10% and 15% alpha
respectively, so an edge reads consistently whether it sits on
`--background` or on a lifted `--card`. That is the one place the palette
uses transparency.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.LinesAndFocus} />

## Dark mode

Every token on this page has a counterpart under `.dark`, switched by a
class rather than a media query, and dark is not a mechanical inversion of
light — surfaces go *up* rather than down, and strong fills get lighter so
their foregrounds flip to dark text. The Light/Dark columns in the
contrast table below cover both.

The mechanism, the three places an inversion would have gone wrong, and
how to follow the OS setting are on their own page:
**[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)**.

## Contrast

Measured, not assumed — every pair below is computed from the OKLCH
values in `tokens.css`. WCAG AA wants 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for UI
component boundaries such as a focus ring.

| Pair | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `background` / `foreground` | 19.28:1 | 19.28:1 |
| `card` / `card-foreground` | 20.13:1 | 17.00:1 |
| `popover` / `popover-foreground` | 20.13:1 | 17.00:1 |
| `primary` / `primary-foreground` | 5.03:1 | 6.79:1 |
| `secondary` / `secondary-foreground` | 16.13:1 | 14.07:1 |
| `accent` / `accent-foreground` | 16.13:1 | 14.07:1 |
| `destructive` / `destructive-foreground` | 4.56:1 | 6.19:1 |
| `muted` / `muted-foreground` | 4.60:1 | 5.64:1 |
| `background` / `muted-foreground` | 4.85:1 | 7.73:1 |
| `background` / `ring` | 6.54:1 | 7.63:1 |

Measured on the defaults: blue accent, gray gray. The `primary` row is the default blue accent. Every one of the seventeen
accents is measured the same way and clears 4.5:1 for its own label — see
[Overview → Accent color](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs).

**`--muted-foreground` on `--muted` is 4.60:1 in light mode**, the
tightest pair it forms. It used to be 4.34:1, under AA: gray-500 on every
ramp has since been darkened to the lightest value that clears 4.6:1 on
its own gray-100, so muted text can now sit on a muted fill. On the page background, where secondary
text usually lives, the same token is 4.85:1.

**`--subtle-foreground` is a step between body text and muted text**
(gray-600 light, gray-300 dark): navigation labels that should recede
until hovered or current, as in the Claude apps' sidebar. It reads about
7.5:1 on the light page, so it is body-safe; use `--muted-foreground` for
genuinely secondary text.

**`--surface-subtle` is a filled panel that muted text can sit on.**
Muted text reads 4.85:1 on it (gray-50) and 5.64:1 on gray-800 in dark — a step off `--card` so a filled panel still reads as filled. The build
measures `--muted-foreground` on `--background`, `--card`,
`--surface-subtle` and `--muted` in both modes on all nine gray ramps, and
stops if any pair drops under 4.5:1. The tightest is neutral on `--muted`,
at 4.60:1.

**`--control-border` outlines a checkbox, radio or switch track.** Those
controls have nothing else that shows they are there, so WCAG 1.4.11 wants
3:1 against the page — and `--input` (gray-200) is about 1.3:1. The build
measures it on all nine gray ramps.

**`--field-border` is the text-field edge** (gray-300 light, white 18%
dark), about 1.5:1: the light hairline of the Claude apps, and a
deliberate exception to 3:1 for fields only. Fields lean on a white
`--card` fill, a faint drop, the label and the focus ring instead. A
product that needs 3:1 sets `--field-border: var(--control-border)`.

**`--primary-text` is the brand hue as text** — an outlined or ghost
primary button. The solid is picked for its label, not for being read on
the page, and amber-500 on white is barely 2:1, so the build measures a
third step per accent that clears 4.5:1 against the page.

**Two values are deliberately off the beaten path.** `--ring` follows the
accent at its `-700` step rather than being a neutral, because a focus
indicator has to clear 3:1 against the page under WCAG 1.4.11 and the
lighter solids miss it — yellow-600 measures 2.93:1, so the ring uses a
step darker than the fill for every accent.
And dark `--destructive-foreground` is neutral-900 rather than near-white:
dark mode inverts the destructive fill to red-400, and near-white on
red-400 is 2.77:1, which makes the label of a destructive button in dark
mode fail AA outright.

## Status

Four fixed hues for messages about state: `info` (blue), `success`
(green), `warning` (amber), `danger` (red). Like `--destructive`, they do
not follow the accent. Each comes as four tokens:

| Token | Use | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--{status}` | Solid fill | 600 (green 700, amber 500) | 400 |
| `--{status}-foreground` | Label on the solid | neutral-50 (amber: neutral-900) | neutral-900 |
| `--{status}-subtle` | Tinted fill | 100 | 950 |
| `--{status}-text` | Text, icon and border on the tint or the page | 800 | 300 |

The steps are pinned by hand, so `npm run tokens` measures them and fails
the build if any pair drops under 4.5:1:

| Pair | info | success | warning | danger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| label on solid, light | 5.03:1 | 4.73:1 | 8.35:1 | 4.56:1 |
| text on subtle, light | 7.25:1 | 6.45:1 | 6.41:1 | 6.86:1 |
| text on page, light | 8.84:1 | 7.09:1 | 7.13:1 | 8.37:1 |
| label on solid, dark | 6.79:1 | 10.09:1 | 10.43:1 | 6.19:1 |
| text on subtle, dark | 8.13:1 | 10.67:1 | 10.37:1 | 8.40:1 |
| text on page, dark | 10.93:1 | 14.16:1 | 13.69:1 | 10.30:1 |

`danger` and `destructive` share red-600 but mean different things:
`destructive` is an action that destroys, `danger` is a state that is
wrong. Keep them apart so either can move without the other.

## Color is never the only signal

`--destructive` on a button does not say what will be destroyed, and a red
badge means nothing to a reader who cannot distinguish it from a neutral
one. Pair color with words, an icon, or a shape every time it carries
meaning. The contrast numbers above are a floor, not a design review.

## Where the values come from

**Every value is a step off a published ramp, digit for digit.** Nothing
here was hand-picked or eyeballed. Two ramps feed the palette and each is
swappable on its own: an **accent** (blue by default) for `--primary` and
`--ring`, and a **gray** (the `gray` ramp by default) for everything structural.

| Token | Light | Dark | Driven by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `background` | gray-50 | gray-950 | gray |
| `foreground` | gray-950 | gray-50 | gray |
| `card`, `popover` | white | gray-900 | gray |
| `card-foreground`, `popover-foreground` | gray-950 | gray-50 | gray |
| `primary` | accent-600 | accent-400 | **accent** |
| `primary-foreground` | white or near-black | near-black | **accent** |
| `secondary`, `muted`, `accent` | gray-100 | gray-800 | gray |
| `secondary-foreground`, `accent-foreground` | gray-900 | gray-50 | gray |
| `selected` | gray-200 | white 10% | gray |
| `hover-overlay` | black 5% | white 6% | fixed |
| `muted-foreground` | gray-500 | gray-400 | gray |
| `subtle-foreground` | gray-600 | gray-300 | gray |
| `surface-subtle` | gray-50 | gray-800 | gray |
| `destructive` | red-600 | red-400 | fixed |
| `destructive-foreground` | neutral-50 | neutral-900 | fixed |
| `border`, `input` | gray-200 | white 10% / 15% | gray |
| `field-border` | gray-300 | white 18% | gray |
| `control-border` | gray-500 | gray-400 | gray |
| `ring` | accent-700 | accent-400 | **accent** |
| `primary-text` | first of accent-600…900 at 4.5:1 on the light page | first of accent-400…200 at 4.5:1 on the dark page | **accent** |

The light accent step is `-600` for most hues but `-700` for sky, fuchsia,
pink and rose, and the label is white or near-black depending on which one
clears 4.5:1 on that fill — the warm hues take dark labels. Exceptions to
the ramp rule: light `--card`/`--popover` (pure white, so a panel reads
lighter than the gray-50 page) and dark `--border`/`--input`/`--selected`, and `--hover-overlay` in both
(alpha, so they work over any surface — the sidebar's hover sits on
`--surface-subtle`, which in dark equals the opaque `--accent` fill).

`--destructive` deliberately does **not** follow the accent. A status
colour that changes with the brand stops being a status.

## Naming

Token names describe a **role**, not a property or a color. `--primary` is
not "the brand color" and `--destructive` is not "red"; they are the
default action and the dangerous one. The names are also the common
contract most token-based kits share, which is what lets a component
copied out of Zweihänder resolve against tokens a target project already
has instead of arriving with its own private palette.

Figma, by contrast, conventionally names tokens by property —
`bg/primary`, `text/primary`, `border/default`. Those do not map one to
one: Figma's `text/primary` is this system's `--foreground`, and its
`bg/primary` is `--background`. Neither is `--primary`. Worth pinning down
before any Figma sync, since the collision is silent.

## Primitives

The full underlying palette — 22 hues × 11 shades. None of these
classes are referenced anywhere in the kit, so they are force-generated by
an `@source inline(...)` directive in `src/index.css` purely so this page
can render them.

This is raw material, not a palette to build UI from. Reach for a
primitive when you are defining the *next* semantic token; if a primitive
shows up in a component, a token is missing.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Primitives} />

## Customization

Swap the raw values in `:root` and `.dark` in `src/tokens.css`. Nothing
that reads `var(--primary)` or `var(--muted-foreground)` changes, because
every rule points at the variable rather than the value.

Two things to carry through a rebrand: re-measure the pairs in the
contrast table — a brand hue at the same *lightness* as neutral-900 will
not necessarily hit the same ratios — and keep light and dark as separate
decisions. Lifting a brand color for dark mode by reusing the light value
is what produces the 2.77:1 failure documented above.

Projects that install through the registry get these values merged into
their own stylesheet; projects on the npm package import
`zweihander/tokens.css` and override afterwards.

const TOKENS = [
  {
    token: '--cursor-button',
    value: 'default',
    usage: 'Button, and anything that acts on the current page',
    note: "Matches the browser's own convention: an interactive element that doesn't navigate keeps the regular arrow, not a hand.",
    demo: <Button>Button</Button>,
  },
  {
    token: '--cursor-link',
    value: 'pointer',
    usage: 'A Button rendered as a real link',
    note: 'A Button with href renders a real <a href>, which navigates — so it keeps the hand the browser gives every other link.',
    demo: <Button href="#cursors">Link</Button>,
  },
  {
    token: '--cursor-disabled',
    value: 'not-allowed',
    usage: 'A disabled control that stays hoverable',
    note: 'TextInput uses this. Button does not — its disabled state is pointer-events: none, so it is never hovered and a cursor there would be dead CSS.',
    demo: (
      <div style={{ width: '9rem' }}>
        <TextInput aria-label="Disabled" placeholder="Disabled" disabled isFullWidth />
      </div>
    ),
  },
] as const

function CursorTokens() {

      {TOKENS.map(({ token, value, usage, note, demo }) => (
        <div
          key={token}
          className={docs.card}
          style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', gap: 'var(--space-2)' }}
        >
          <div style={{ display: 'flex', alignItems: 'center', gap: 'var(--space-4)' }}>
            {/* Real components rather than a styled div, so what you hover is
                what ships — a div with cursor set on it would demonstrate the
                token but not that any component actually reads it. */}
            <div style={{ width: '9rem', flexShrink: 0 }}>{demo}</div>
            <div style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column' }}>
              <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body)' }}>
                {token}
              </span>

            </div>
          </div>
          <p className={docs.note}>
            <strong style={{ color: 'var(--foreground)', fontWeight: 500 }}>{usage}.</strong> {note}
          </p>
        </div>

}

# Cursors Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do not get ...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as CursorsStories from './Cursors.stories'

<Meta of={CursorsStories} />

# Cursors

Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do
not get `cursor: pointer`. Links do.**

## The convention

`cursor: pointer` means "this navigates" — it is the hand that appears
over a link. Browsers have never applied it to `<button>`, `<select>` or a
checkbox, and neither does this kit. Interactive elements that act on the
current page keep the regular arrow; only a link gets the hand. This is a
deliberate departure from the very common `button { cursor: pointer }`
reset.

It is worth knowing the argument on the other side: a large body of
usability opinion holds that the hand cursor is now such a widespread
affordance for "clickable" that removing it costs more than the semantic
purity gains. If your product takes that view, this is a one-line change —
see **Customization** below. The point of making it a token is that it is
one line, in one place, rather than a decision re-litigated per component.

<Canvas of={CursorsStories.Tokens} />

## `--cursor-button`

`default` — the regular arrow. Applied by Button.

Note this changes nothing visually today: a native `<button>` already
shows the arrow. **The token's job is not its current value; it is that
the value is reachable.** Without it, switching the kit to `pointer` means
editing every component; with it, it is one declaration.

## `--cursor-link`

`pointer` — the hand.

This one exists because the convention above has a second half that is
easy to state and easy to get wrong. Button takes `href`, so it can
render as a real `<a href>` — and when it did, it inherited
`--cursor-button` and lost the hand that the browser gives every other
link on the page. A link styled as a button is still a link.

```css
a[href].button {
  cursor: var(--cursor-link);
}
```

The `a[href]` part is doing real work. An `<a>` without `href` is not a
link and browsers do not give it the hand either, so matching on the
attribute rather than the element keeps the rule honest.

The distinction the kit draws is navigation versus action, not
appearance: a `<button>` styled as a link would still act on the current
page, so it would keep the arrow.

| | Element | Cursor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<Button>` | `<button>` | arrow |
| `<Button href="/x">` | `<a href>` | hand |

The Button `Href` story asserts this, and compares against a bare
`<a href>` rather than the literal `pointer` — so overriding
`--cursor-link` moves the assertion with it instead of breaking it.

## `--cursor-disabled`

`not-allowed` — used by TextInput, and **not** by Button. That asymmetry
is not an oversight.

A disabled `<input>` stays hit-testable, so a cursor set on it renders and
the user gets feedback on hover. Button's disabled state is
`pointer-events: none`, which makes the element untargetable; an
untargetable element is never hovered, so a cursor there would be dead
CSS. The `pointer-events: none` is not incidental — because Button
can render as an `<a>`, which ignores the `disabled` attribute entirely. Blocking pointer events is what actually disables it
in that case.

So the token applies to the pattern where a control stays hoverable while
disabled — including a control deliberately wrapped so a tooltip can
explain *why*. That trade-off, between a disabled control you can
interrogate and one that is inert, is a real design choice, and the two
components here happen to sit on opposite sides of it.

## Adding tokens

A mature system ends up with a token per interactive component —
checkboxes, menu items, radios, switches, slider thumbs. This kit has
three, because it has two components and one of them can render as two
different things.

**Add a token when the component that needs it is built, not before.** A
`--cursor-slider-thumb` with no Slider is a value nobody can verify and
that the eventual Slider may not want.

## Customization

All three are plain CSS keywords, not colors, so they override like any
other custom property:

```css
:root {
  --cursor-button: pointer;
}
```

Load any override after Zweihänder's own stylesheet so the cascade picks it
up. Setting `--cursor-button: pointer` is the one-line version of adopting
the mainstream convention; it leaves `--cursor-link` alone, which is
already `pointer`, so the two simply converge.

# Dark mode Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the light v...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as DarkModeStories from './DarkMode.stories'

<Meta of={DarkModeStories} />

# Dark mode

Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the
light values on `:root, .light` and the dark values on `.dark`, and
Every rule in the kit reads those variables, so the class is the only
switch there is.

Nothing is automatic about it. Adding `class="dark"` to `<html>` is what
switches the document; without that, a device set to dark mode gets the
light theme. That is the trade — see **Following the system** below.

<Canvas of={DarkModeStories.SideBySide} />

## Components don't know about it

No component stylesheet — `Button.module.css`, `InputField.module.css` or any other — mentions `.dark`.
They write `background: var(--primary)`, and it is the variable that
changes; the rule is identical in both modes.

This is the main reason to reach for a token rather than a literal. A
hard-coded `#0a0a0a` is near-black in both modes and needs a `.dark`
override beside it to survive a theme switch; `var(--primary)` needs
nothing. Every theme conditional in a codebase is a place a value was
hardcoded and then patched.

## Dark is not an inversion

Flipping lightness would produce the wrong result in three places, and the
palette deliberately doesn't:

- **`--background` is neutral-950, not black.** A pure-black page makes
  the halation around light text worse and leaves no room to sit a surface
  *below* the page level.
- **Surfaces go up, not down.** `--card` and `--popover` are a step
  *lighter* than the page in dark mode and identical to it in light mode.
  Elevation in dark mode is carried by lightness, because a drop shadow
  has almost nothing left to darken (see
  [Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)).
- **Strong fills become light, so their labels become dark.**
  `--primary` goes from near-black to near-white, and
  `--primary-foreground` inverts with it. `--destructive` does the same,
  red-600 to red-400 — which is exactly where the palette's one contrast
  bug lived: keeping the near-white label on the lightened red measured
  2.77:1. It is now neutral-900 at 6.19:1. Inverting a fill without
  inverting its foreground is the single easiest dark-mode mistake to
  make.

Full measurements for both modes are in
[Color → Contrast](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs).

## Alpha for edges

`--border` and `--input` are the one place the palette uses transparency:
opaque neutral-200 in light, `white / 10%` and `white / 15%` in dark. An
opaque dark border would have to be re-chosen for every surface it sits
on; a translucent white edge lightens whatever is underneath, so the same
token reads correctly on `--background` and on a lifted `--card`.

## Scoping

`Theme` switches an appearance for a subtree rather than the document —
a dark footer on a light page, a light popover inside a dark shell. See
[Overview → Nesting](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) for how the
nesting resolves and the one caveat that comes with it.

```tsx
<Theme appearance="dark">
  <Footer />
</Theme>
```

## Following the system

The kit ships no `prefers-color-scheme` handling, because the choice
between "follow the OS" and "remember what the user picked" belongs to the
app, not the component library. The usual shape:

```ts
const media = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')
const stored = localStorage.getItem('theme') // 'light' | 'dark' | null
const dark = stored ? stored === 'dark' : media.matches
document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark)
```

Two things worth getting right. Run it **before first paint** — in a
blocking inline script in `<head>`, not in a `useEffect` — or the page
renders light and flips, which is the flash every themed site has had at
some point. And keep listening to `media` afterwards so a user changing
their OS setting mid-session is followed, unless they have made an
explicit choice.

In this Storybook, the **Theme** toolbar control does the class toggle for
you; there is no persistence and no system detection.

  gap: 'var(--space-2)',
}

const STEPS = ['radius-sm', 'radius-md', 'radius-lg', 'radius-xl'] as const

function StepScale() {

          <span className={docs.caption}>--{token}</span>
        </div>

}

const INTENTS = [
  { token: 'radius-control', label: 'control', note: 'Button, badge' },
  { token: 'radius-field', label: 'field', note: 'Input, textarea' },
  { token: 'radius-panel', label: 'panel', note: 'Card, dialog' },
] as const

function Intents() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.rowWrap}>
      {INTENTS.map(({ token, label, note }) => (
        <div key={token} style={COL}>
          <div
            style={{
              display: 'flex',
              height: '4rem',
              width: '7rem',
              alignItems: 'center',
              justifyContent: 'center',
              background: 'var(--secondary)',
              color: 'var(--secondary-foreground)',
              fontSize: 'var(--text-body)',
              borderRadius: `var(--${token})`,
            }}
          >
            {label}
          </div>
          <span className={docs.caption}>--{token}</span>
          <span className={docs.caption}>{note}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

const PRESETS: RadiusPreset[] = ['none', 'small', 'medium', 'large', 'full']

function PresetRow({ preset }: { preset: RadiusPreset }) {
  return (
    <Theme radius={preset} className={docs.stack}>
      <span className={docs.caption}>radius="{preset}"</span>
      <div style={{ display: 'flex', flexWrap: 'wrap', alignItems: 'center', gap: 'var(--space-3)' }}>
        <Button>Button</Button>
        <div style={{ width: '10rem' }}>
          <TextInput aria-label="Input" placeholder="Input" isFullWidth />
        </div>
        <div
          data-panel
          style={{
            border: '1px solid var(--border)',
            background: 'var(--card)',
            color: 'var(--card-foreground)',
            padding: 'var(--space-2) var(--space-4)',
            fontSize: 'var(--text-body)',
            borderRadius: 'var(--radius-panel)',
          }}
        >
          Panel
        </div>
      </div>
    </Theme>
  )
}

// Narrative and prose live in Radius.mdx.
const meta = {
  title: 'Foundations/Radius',
  parameters: { layout: 'padded' },
} satisfies Meta

export default meta
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Presets: Story = {
  render: () => (
    <div className={docs.stackWide}>
      {PRESETS.map((preset) => (
        <PresetRow key={preset} preset={preset} />
      ))}
    </div>
  ),
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    const px = (el: Element) => Number.parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el).borderRadius)
    const scopeFor = (preset: string) =>
      canvas.getByText(`radius="${preset}"`).parentElement as HTMLElement
    const parts = (preset: string) => {
      const scope = scopeFor(preset)
      return {
        control: px(scope.querySelector('button')!),
        // The field's corner is on the box that draws it, not the bare <input>.
        field: px(scope.querySelector('input')!.parentElement!),
        panel: px(scope.querySelector('[data-panel]')!),
      }
    }

    // none flattens everything.
    const none = parts('none')
    await expect(none.control).toBe(0)
    await expect(none.field).toBe(0)
    await expect(none.panel).toBe(0)

    const large = parts('large')
    const full = parts('full')

    // full pills the control...
    await expect(full.control).toBeGreaterThan(1000)
    // ...but a field must never reach a pill. The input is 32px tall, so
    // anything at or above 16px is one.
    await expect(full.field).toBeLessThan(16)
    await expect(full.panel).toBeLessThan(1000)
    // ...and it still has to be a step up from large, or "full" would just
    // be "large with a pill button".
    await expect(full.field).toBeGreaterThan(large.field)
    await expect(full.panel).toBeGreaterThan(large.panel)
  },
}

export const Steps: Story = {
  render: () => <StepScale />,
}

export const Intent: Story = {
  render: () => <Intents />,
}

# Radius Rounding is a **single setting**, not a value picked per component. A `radius` pr...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as RadiusStories from './Radius.stories'

<Meta of={RadiusStories} />

# Radius

Rounding is a **single setting**, not a value picked per component. A
`radius` preset on `Theme` rescales everything inside it at once, and
components follow because they reference an *intent* — control, field,
panel — rather than a fixed number.

```tsx
<Theme radius="large">
  <Button>Rounder</Button>
</Theme>
```

## Presets

Five: `none`, `small`, **`medium` (the default)**, `large`, `full`. The
default is set by `--radius-factor: 1` and `--radius-full: 0px` on
`:root`, which is exactly what the `medium` preset writes — so a scope
with no `radius` prop and a scope with `radius="medium"` are identical.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Presets} />

Look at the `full` row. **The button becomes a pill; the input and the
panel get rounder but stop short of one.** That is the whole reason this
is a system rather than a number: a fully rounded text field reads as a
search pill in a form that isn't one, and a fully rounded card stops
looking like a container. Only controls opt all the way in.

`none` flattens every corner in the scope to `0`, including panels.

## How it works

Two variables do the work, both on `:root`:

| Variable | Default | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--radius` | `0.625rem` | you, for the base step |
| `--radius-factor` | `1` | the `radius` preset |
| `--radius-full` | `0px` | the `radius` preset, only at `full` |

Every step is the base multiplied by the factor, so the preset scales the
whole scale rather than replacing it:

| Preset | Factor | `--radius-full` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | `0` | `0px` |
| `small` | `0.5` | `0px` |
| `medium` | `1` | `0px` |
| `large` | `1.5` | `0px` |
| `full` | `1.5` | `9999px` |

The pill is a `max()`. `--radius-control` resolves to
`max(step, var(--radius-full))` — normally the step wins because
`--radius-full` is `0px`, and at the `full` preset the `9999px` wins
instead.

Fields and panels use the same shape with a ceiling wrapped around it:

```css
max(step, min(cap, var(--radius-full)))
```

`min(cap, --radius-full)` is `0px` normally and the cap at `full`, so they
step up with the preset and stop there. Concretely, at the default base:

| Preset | `control` | `field` | `panel` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `small` | 4px | 4px | 7px |
| `medium` | 8px | 8px | 14px |
| `large` | 12px | 12px | 21px |
| `full` | pill | 15px | 27px |

Small (24px) buttons and fields take `--radius-sm` (6px at the default)
instead: the same corner on a box two thirds the height reads as a pill.

The default input is 32px tall, so a pill would be 16px — `field` at
`full` lands under that on purpose, and a test asserts it.

## Intent tokens

What components actually use.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Intent} />

| Token | Used by | Pills at `full` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--radius-control` | Button, and future badges/chips | yes |
| `--radius-field` | TextInput, and future textareas/selects | no |
| `--radius-panel` | future cards, dialogs, popovers | no |

A new component should pick the intent that matches its shape, not a step.
Getting this wrong is invisible at the default preset and only shows up
when someone sets `radius="full"` — which is exactly the kind of bug a
token system exists to prevent.

## Steps

The raw scale — `--radius-sm` through `--radius-xl` — for anything that is
genuinely decorative rather than a control, field or panel.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Steps} />

These follow the preset like everything else, so a decorative corner in
application code stays in step with the controls beside it.

A genuinely circular element — an avatar, a status dot — should use
`border-radius: 50%` rather than a token. `--radius-full` is the pill
switch, not a "make this round" value: read directly it is `0` at every
preset except `full`.

## Scoping and overriding

Presets nest, and `Theme` takes a `render` prop, so a single component can
opt out without a wrapper element:

```tsx
<Theme radius="full" render={<Button />}>
  Just this one is a pill
</Theme>
```

For a value the presets don't cover, set the variables directly — `tokens`
is applied after the preset, so it wins:

```tsx
<Theme radius="large" tokens={{ 'radius-factor': '2.4' }}>
```

Globally, change the base in CSS and leave the factor to the presets:

```css
:root {
  --radius: 1rem;
}
```

## One caveat about the base

The steps are offsets from the base — `sm` is `base − 4px`, not
`base × 0.6` — so a base far below the default degenerates. At
`--radius: 0.25rem` (4px) the steps are `0 / 2 / 4 / 8px` and `sm`
collapses to a square corner.

The factor does not have this problem, because it multiplies the finished
step. Prefer moving the preset over moving the base, and if the base does
need to change substantially, switch the four `calc()`s in `tokens.css`
from offsets to ratios.
